title: Urine formation and fluid, electrolyte and blood-pressure control
blurb: Explain filtration, reabsorption and secretion, and predict how ADH, aldosterone, RAAS and ANP change urine and blood pressure.
question: After a long, hot shift without drinking, a nursing assistant notices his urine is dark and scant. Which hormone is responsible, where in the nephron does it act, and what does it change?

teach.body: Formally, urine forms by glomerular filtration, tubular reabsorption and tubular secretion, so the amount excreted equals filtered minus reabsorbed plus secreted. In plain English: the kidney pushes a large volume of plasma fluid out of the blood, takes back almost everything useful, then actively adds a few extra wastes. Whatever is left in the tubule at the end is urine.

steps.label: Filtration
steps.sub: Renal corpuscle: blood pressure pushes fluid into the capsule

steps.label: Reabsorption
steps.sub: Filtrate to blood: about 99% is taken back

steps.label: Secretion
steps.sub: Blood to filtrate: H+, K+, creatinine, drugs, toxins

teach.caption: Filtered: water and small solutes (glucose, amino acids, ions, urea). Not filtered: blood cells and large plasma proteins.

head: Segment
Main action
rows: Reabsorbs the most: all glucose and amino acids, ~65% of Na+ and water, bicarbonate
Impermeable to water; pumps out Na+ and Cl-
teach.caption: The ascending limb builds the salty medullary gradient that lets the collecting duct concentrate urine.

head: Normally present
Not normally present
teach.caption: Normal urine is pale yellow (urochrome), pH range about 4.5–8, specific gravity about 1.005–1.030. Urea is made in the liver.

head: Hormone
From
Effect
rows: Aquaporins in collecting duct: less, concentrated urine
DCT/collecting duct reabsorb Na+ (water follows), secrete K+
More Na+ and water lost; BP falls
More Ca2+ reabsorbed in the DCT
teach.caption: ADH is made in the hypothalamus and released by the posterior pituitary. Alcohol inhibits ADH, which is why it increases urine output.
The kidneys can also make glucose (gluconeogenesis) during fasting.

teach.body: Ethan, a nursing assistant, works a hot 12-hour shift and barely drinks. His blood becomes more concentrated, so his posterior pituitary releases more ADH. ADH inserts aquaporins in his collecting ducts, so more water returns to the blood. Result: a small volume of dark, concentrated urine. If his blood pressure also dropped, renin would trigger RAAS, and aldosterone would make his DCT reabsorb more sodium, with water following.

teach.text: ADH acts on the COLLECTING DUCT and DECREASES urine volume. Aldosterone reabsorbs Na+ and SECRETES K+. Renin is an ENZYME from juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney, not an adrenal hormone. Most reabsorption happens in the PCT.

items: Excreted = filtered minus reabsorbed plus secreted.
PCT reabsorbs the most, including all glucose and amino acids normally.
Glucose, protein, blood cells and ketones in urine are abnormal.
ADH: keep water. Aldosterone: keep Na+, lose K+. ANP: lose Na+ and water. PTH: keep Ca2+.
RAAS: renin, angiotensin I, ACE, angiotensin II; BP rises.

summary: You can now describe filtration, reabsorption and secretion, say what normal urine contains, and identify where the PCT, loop and collecting duct do their work. You can also predict how ADH, aldosterone, ANP and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system change urine volume and blood pressure.

A.q: Which part of the nephron reabsorbs the largest share of filtered water and sodium?
A.why: The PCT reabsorbs about 65% of filtered Na+ and water, plus all glucose and amino acids normally.

whyNot.0: The collecting duct fine-tunes water reabsorption under ADH; it handles a much smaller share.
whyNot.1: The ascending limb pumps out Na+ and Cl- but is impermeable to water.
whyNot.3: The DCT fine-tunes reabsorption under hormones such as aldosterone; it is not the main site.

A.q: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) increases water reabsorption mainly by acting on which structure?
A.why: ADH inserts aquaporins (water channels) into the collecting duct, so more water returns to the blood.

whyNot.0: The PCT reabsorbs water without depending on ADH.
whyNot.2: The glomerulus filters blood; ADH does not act there.
whyNot.3: The descending limb is permeable to water already; ADH's target is the collecting duct.

A.q: Which substance is a normal component of urine?
A.why: Urea, made in the liver from ammonia, is the main nitrogenous waste in normal urine.

whyNot.0: Glucose is normally all reabsorbed in the PCT; glucose in urine suggests diabetes mellitus.
whyNot.1: Ketones are not normally present in urine.
whyNot.3: Albumin is a large plasma protein that is not normally filtered.

B.q: Tubular secretion moves substances in which direction, and which is an example?
B.why: Secretion moves substances from the blood into the filtrate; H+, K+, creatinine, drugs and toxins are secreted.

whyNot.1: Filtrate to blood is reabsorption, not secretion.
whyNot.2: Glucose is filtered and then reabsorbed, not secreted.
whyNot.3: Creatinine is secreted into the filtrate, and filtrate to blood is the direction of reabsorption.

B.q: Aldosterone acts on the distal tubule and collecting duct. What is its effect?
B.why: Aldosterone makes the DCT and collecting duct reabsorb sodium (water follows) and secrete potassium.

whyNot.0: The ions are reversed: aldosterone keeps sodium and gets rid of potassium.
whyNot.1: Inserting aquaporins in the collecting duct is the action of ADH.
whyNot.2: Calcium reabsorption in the DCT is driven by PTH, not aldosterone.

B.q: Which statement about glomerular filtration is correct?
options: Active transport pumps plasma proteins into the capsule
Red blood cells and glucose are filtered into the capsule
Blood pressure pushes water and small solutes into the capsule
Filtration takes place as filtrate flows along the nephron loop
B.why: In the renal corpuscle, blood pressure forces water and small solutes (glucose, amino acids, ions, urea) into the glomerular capsule.

whyNot.0: Filtration is driven by blood pressure, and large plasma proteins stay in the blood.
whyNot.1: Glucose is filtered, but red blood cells are too large and stay in the blood.
whyNot.3: Filtration happens in the renal corpuscle; the loop processes filtrate that has already formed.

C.q: Which sequence correctly shows the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system after blood pressure falls?
options: Renin, angiotensin I, ACE, angiotensin II, aldosterone
ACE, angiotensin I, renin, angiotensin II, aldosterone
Renin, angiotensin II, ACE, angiotensin I, aldosterone
Aldosterone, renin, angiotensin I, ACE, angiotensin II
C.why: Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I; ACE converts that to angiotensin II, which triggers aldosterone release.

whyNot.1: Renin acts first; ACE acts on angiotensin I, which renin has to produce.
whyNot.2: Angiotensin I comes before angiotensin II; ACE converts I into II.
whyNot.3: Aldosterone is released at the end, in response to angiotensin II.

C.q: Ethan finishes a hot 12-hour shift having barely had a drink. Which response best describes his kidneys?
options: Less ADH, less water reabsorbed, large dilute urine
More ANP, more sodium lost, large dilute urine
More ADH, aquaporins added to the PCT, large volume of urine
More ADH, more water reabsorbed, small concentrated urine
C.why: Dehydration raises ADH, which adds aquaporins in the collecting duct, so more water is reabsorbed and urine becomes concentrated and scant.

whyNot.0: Dehydration increases ADH; less ADH would produce large, dilute urine.
whyNot.1: ANP promotes sodium and water loss, which would worsen dehydration rather than conserve water.
whyNot.2: ADH acts on the collecting duct, and its effect is a smaller volume of urine.

C.q: Which is NOT an effect of angiotensin II?
C.why: ANP comes from the heart and lowers blood pressure; angiotensin II raises it.

whyNot.0: Angiotensin II constricts blood vessels, raising blood pressure.
whyNot.2: Angiotensin II stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone.
whyNot.3: Angiotensin II stimulates thirst, which increases fluid intake.

reteach.title: Clearing out a closet
reteach.question: Imagine tipping your whole closet onto the bed, putting back what you want and adding a few extra items to the donation bag. How does that match urine formation?

blocks.body: Tipping everything onto the bed is filtration: fast and unselective, except the furniture (blood cells, big proteins) stays put. Putting back what you want is reabsorption, and you put back almost everything. Pulling a few extra things off the shelves for the donation bag is secretion. The bag is urine. The hormones are the person giving orders: ADH says keep more water, aldosterone says keep salt and bag the potassium, ANP says bag more salt and water.

blocks.text: Direction decides the name: filtrate to blood is reabsorption; blood to filtrate is secretion.

explain.body: In the renal corpuscle, blood pressure pushes water and small solutes (glucose, amino acids, ions, urea) into the glomerular capsule. Blood cells and large plasma proteins stay in the blood. GFR is about 125 mL/min, roughly 180 L of filtrate a day.

test.q: Which pair is normally NOT filtered at the glomerulus?
options: Urea and sodium and chloride ions
test.why: Blood cells and large plasma proteins are too big to pass the glomerular filter.

whyNot.0: Glucose and amino acids are small and are filtered, then reabsorbed in the PCT.
whyNot.1: Urea and ions are small solutes that pass into the filtrate.
whyNot.3: Water and potassium ions are freely filtered.

explain.body: About 99% of filtrate returns to the blood. The PCT does the most: all glucose and amino acids normally, about 65% of Na+ and water, and bicarbonate. The descending loop loses water; the ascending loop pumps out Na+ and Cl-. The DCT and collecting duct fine-tune under hormones.

test.q: Glucose appears in the urine of a patient with diabetes mellitus. Why is this abnormal?
options: Glucose is normally too large to be filtered
The PCT normally reabsorbs all filtered glucose
ADH normally carries glucose back into blood
The loop of Henle normally secretes it into blood
test.why: Glucose is filtered, but the PCT normally reabsorbs all of it, so none should reach the urine.

whyNot.0: Glucose is small and is filtered; it is normally reabsorbed afterwards.
whyNot.2: ADH controls water reabsorption in the collecting duct, not glucose.
whyNot.3: Moving substances back into the blood is reabsorption, and glucose is reclaimed in the PCT, not the loop.

explain.body: Secretion adds H+, K+, creatinine, drugs and toxins to the filtrate, mainly in the PCT and DCT. Normal urine is about 95% water with urea, creatinine, uric acid and ions, pale yellow, pH about 6. Glucose, protein, blood cells, ketones and bilirubin are not normally present.

test.q: Which substance is NOT normally found in urine?
test.why: Ketones are not a normal component of urine.

whyNot.0: Urea is the main nitrogenous waste in normal urine.
whyNot.1: Creatinine is secreted and excreted normally.
whyNot.2: Uric acid is a normal urine waste.

explain.body: ADH adds aquaporins in the collecting duct (less urine). Aldosterone reabsorbs Na+ and secretes K+. Low BP triggers RAAS: renin, angiotensin I, ACE, angiotensin II, then vasoconstriction, aldosterone, ADH and thirst. ANP from the heart does the opposite, lowering BP.

test.q: Which hormone makes the kidneys excrete more sodium and water, lowering blood pressure?
test.why: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), from the heart, increases sodium and water loss, so blood pressure falls.

whyNot.1: ADH increases water reabsorption, which raises blood volume.
whyNot.2: Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption, with water following.
whyNot.3: Renin starts RAAS, which raises blood pressure.
